recommendation_tables.title: Section 5. Recommendation Table 6 — Recommendations for the role of computed tomography, nuclear imaging, and magnetic resonance in infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: Cardiac CTA is recommended in patients with possible NVE to detect valvular lesions and confirm the diagnosis of IE.
[18F]FDG-PET/CT(A) and cardiac CTA are recommended in possible PVE to detect valvular lesions and confirm the diagnosis of IE.
[18F]FDG-PET/CT(A) may be considered in possible CIED-related IE to confirm the diagnosis of IE.
Cardiac CTA is recommended in NVE and PVE to diagnose paravalvular or periprosthetic complications in which echocardiography is inconclusive.
Brain and whole-body imaging (CT, [18F]FDG-PET/CT, and/or MRI) are recommended in symptomatic patients with NVE and PVE to detect peripheral lesions or add minor diagnostic criteria.
WBC SPECT/CT should be considered in patients with high clinical suspicion of PVE when echocardiography is negative or inconclusive and when PET/CT is unavailable.
Brain and whole-body imaging (CT, [18F]FDG-PET/CT, and MRI) in NVE and PVE may be considered for screening of peripheral lesions in asymptomatic patients.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 7. Recommendation Table 11 — Recommendations for outpatient antibiotic treatment of infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: Outpatient parenteral antibiotic treatment should be considered in patients with left-sided IE caused by Streptococcus spp., E. faecalis, S. aureus, or CoNS who were receiving appropriate i.v. antibiotic treatment for at least 10 days (or at least 7 days after cardiac surgery), are clinically stable, and who do not show signs of abscess formation or valve abnormalities requiring surgery on TOE.

Outpatient parenteral antibiotic treatment is not recommended in patients with IE caused by highly difficult-to-treat microorganisms, liver cirrhosis (Child–Pugh B or C), severe cerebral nervous system emboli, untreated large extracardiac abscesses, heart valve complications, or other severe conditions requiring surgery, severe post-surgical complications, and in PWID-related IE.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 9. Recommendation Table 13 — Recommendations for the treatment of neurological complications of infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: In embolic stroke, mechanical thrombectomy may be considered if the expertise is available in a timely manner.
Thrombolytic therapy is not recommended in embolic stroke due to IE.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 9. Recommendation Table 14 — Recommendations for pacemaker implantation in patients with complete atrioventricular block and infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: Immediate epicardial pacemaker implantation should be considered in patients undergoing surgery for valvular IE and complete AVB if one of the following predictors of persistent AVB is present: pre-operative conduction abnormality, S. aureus infection, aortic root abscess, tricuspid valve involvement, or previous valvular surgery.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 9. Recommendation Table 15 — Recommendations for patients with musculoskeletal manifestations of infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: MRI or PET/CT is recommended in patients with suspected spondylodiscitis and vertebral osteomyelitis complicating IE.
TTE/TOE is recommended to rule out IE in patients with spondylodiscitis and/or septic arthritis with positive blood cultures for typical IE microorganisms.

More than 6-week antibiotic therapy should be considered in patients with osteoarticular IE-related lesions caused by difficult-to-treat microorganisms, such as S. aureus or Candida spp., and/or complicated with severe vertebral destruction or abscesses.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 10. Recommendation Table 16 — Recommendations for pre-operative coronary anatomy assessment in patients requiring surgery for infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: In haemodynamically stable patients with aortic valve vegetations who require cardiac surgery and are high risk of CAD, a high-resolution multislice coronary CTA is recommended.
Invasive coronary angiography is recommended in patients requiring heart surgery who are high risk of CAD, in the absence of aortic valve vegetations.
In emergency situations, valvular surgery without pre-operative coronary anatomy assessment regardless of CAD risk should be considered.
Invasive coronary angiography may be considered despite the presence of aortic valve vegetations in selected patients with known CAD or at high risk of significant obstructive CAD.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 10. Recommendation Table 17 — Indications and timing of cardiac surgery after neurological complications in active infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: In patients with intracranial haemorrhage and unstable clinical status due to HF, uncontrolled infection, or persistent high embolic risk, urgent or emergency surgery should be considered weighing the likelihood of a meaningful neurological outcome.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 11. Recommendation Table 18 — Recommendations for post-discharge follow-up

rows.recommendation: Patient education on the risk of recurrence and preventive measures, with emphasis on dental health, and based on the individual risk profile, is recommended during follow-up.
Addiction treatment for patients following PWID-related IE is recommended.
Cardiac rehabilitation including physical exercise training should be considered in clinically stable patients based on an individual assessment.

rows.recommendation: Surgery is recommended for early PVE (within 6 months of valve surgery) with new valve replacement and complete debridement.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 12. Recommendation Table 20 — Recommendations for cardiovascular implanted electronic device-related infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: Complete system extraction without delay is recommended in patients with definite CIED-related IE under initial empirical antibiotic therapy.
Extension of antibiotic treatment of CIED-related endocarditis to (4–)6 weeks following device extraction should be considered in the presence of septic emboli or prosthetic valves.
Use of an antibiotic envelope may be considered in select high-risk patients undergoing CIED reimplantation to reduce risk of infection.

In non-S. aureus CIED-related endocarditis without valve involvement or lead vegetations, and if follow-up blood cultures are negative without septic emboli, 2 weeks of antibiotic treatment may be considered following device extraction.
Removal of CIED after a single positive blood culture, with no other clinical evidence of infection, is not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 12. Recommendation Table 21 — Recommendations for the surgical treatment of right-sided infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: Tricuspid valve repair should be considered instead of valve replacement, when possible.

Surgery should be considered in patients with right-side IE who are receiving appropriate antibiotic therapy and present persistent bacteraemia/sepsis after at least 1 week of appropriate antibiotic therapy.
Prophylactic placement of an epicardial pacing lead should be considered at the time of tricuspid valve surgical procedures.
Debulking of right intra-atrial septic masses by aspiration may be considered in select patients who are high risk of surgery.

rows.supporting_text: TOE should be considered in patients with suspected IE, even in cases with positive TTE, except in isolated right-sided native valve IE with good quality TTE examination and unequivocal echocardiographic finding.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 8. Recommendation Table 12 — Recommendations for the main indications of surgery in infective endocarditis (native valve endocarditis and prosthetic valve endocarditis)

rows.supporting_text: Aortic or mitral NVE with vegetations >10 mm associated with severe valve stenosis or regurgitation, and low operative risk (urgent surgery should be considered).

rows.recommendation: Urgent surgery may be considered in aortic or mitral IE with vegetation ≥10 mm and without severe valve dysfunction or without clinical evidence of embolism and low surgical risk.
rows.supporting_text: Aortic or mitral NVE or PVE with isolated large vegetations (>15 mm) and no other indication for surgery (urgent surgery may be considered).

recommendation_tables.title: Section 9. Recommendation Table 13 — Recommendations for the treatment of neurological complications of infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: Brain CT or MRA is recommended in patients with IE and suspected infective cerebral aneurysms.
rows.supporting_text: Intracranial infectious aneurysms should be looked for in patients with IE and neurological symptoms. CT or MRA should be considered for diagnosis.

rows.recommendation: If non-invasive techniques are negative and the suspicion of infective aneurysm remains, invasive angiography should be considered.
rows.supporting_text: If non-invasive techniques are negative and the suspicion of intracranial aneurysm remains, conventional angiography should be considered.

recommendation_tables.title: Section 12. Recommendation Table 20 — Recommendations for cardiovascular implanted electronic device-related infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended before device implantation.
Antibiotic prophylaxis covering S. aureus is recommended for CIED implantation.

TOE is recommended in patients with suspected cardiac device-related infective endocarditis with positive or negative blood cultures, independent of the results of TTE, to evaluate lead-related endocarditis and heart valve infection.
TTE and TOE are both recommended in case of suspected CIED-related IE to identify vegetations.
In patients with NVE or PVE and an intracardiac device with no evidence of associated device infection, complete hardware extraction may be considered.
Complete CIED extraction should be considered in case of valvular IE, even without definite lead involvement, taking into account the identified pathogen and requirement for valve surgery.

rows.recommendation: Complete hardware removal should be considered on the basis of occult infection without another apparent source of infection.

In cases of possible CIED-related IE or occult Gram-positive bacteraemia or fungaemia, complete system removal should be considered in case bacteraemia/fungaemia persists after a course of antimicrobial therapy.

In cases of possible CIED-related IE with occult Gram-negative bacteraemia, complete system removal may be considered in case of persistent/relapsing bacteraemia after a course of antimicrobial therapy.
When indicated, definite reimplantation should be postponed if possible, to allow a few days or weeks of antibiotic therapy.

If CIED reimplantation is indicated after extraction for CIED-related IE, it is recommended to be performed at a site distant from the previous generator, as late as possible, once signs and symptoms of infection have abated and until blood cultures are negative for at least 72 h in the absence of vegetations, and negative for at least 2 weeks if vegetations were visualized.

section_headings: 3.2. Populations at risk of infective endocarditis
content.narrative_summary: This section reviews evidence on the efficacy and risks of antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis (IE), citing meta-analyses that show reductions in bacteraemia but no definitive protective effect in case–control studies, and notes concerns about anaphylaxis and antibiotic resistance. Following a Task Force review of studies published after 2015, the risk categories for IE were revised. Section 3.2 outlines high-risk groups for whom prophylaxis is recommended—including patients with prior IE, those with prosthetic valves or repair materials, congenital heart disease, and ventricular assist devices—and intermediate-risk groups including rheumatic heart disease, degenerative valve diseases, certain congenital valve abnormalities, cardiovascular implantable electronic devices, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Table 5
figures_tables_algorithms.title: General prevention measures to be followed in patients at high and intermediate risk of infective endocarditis
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
1. Patients should be encouraged to maintain twice daily tooth cleaning and to seek professional dental cleaning and follow-up at least twice yearly for high-risk patients and yearly for others.
2. Strict cutaneous hygiene, including optimized treatment of chronic skin conditions.
3. Disinfection of wounds.
4. Curative antibiotics for any focus of bacterial infection.
5. No self-medication with antibiotics.
6. Strict infection control measures for any at-risk procedure.
7. Discouragement of piercing and tattooing.
8. Limitation of infusion catheters and invasive procedures, when possible. Strict adherence to care bundles for central and peripheral cannulae should be performed.

content.narrative_summary: This page continues the discussion that antibiotic prophylaxis is not routinely recommended at intermediate risk of infective endocarditis except on an individual basis. In solid organ transplant recipients, IE is mainly nosocomial, most often due to Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus fumigatus, with oral streptococci being an infrequent cause and fungal IE associated with high mortality. Section 3.3 outlines situations requiring antibiotic prophylaxis, recommending it for patients at high risk undergoing at-risk dental procedures and summarizing regimens in Table 6. Non-dental procedures are introduced with no convincing evidence linking them to IE.

content.narrative_summary: The prose describes the composition and resources of a Heart Valve Centre and the Endocarditis Team for treating infective endocarditis. Core members include cardiologists, cardiovascular surgeons, infectious disease specialists, and microbiologists. Additional specialists—such as pathologists, critical care specialists, cardiac anaesthesiologists, interventional cardiologists, neurologists, neurosurgeons, pharmacologists, radiologists, nuclear medicine specialists, nephrologists, geriatricians, and multidisciplinary addiction medicine teams—should be available for consultation. The Endocarditis Team frequently assesses complex and high-risk patients, may require difficult therapeutic and legal decisions, and relies on advanced cardiovascular imaging in diagnosis.

content.narrative_summary: Laboratory investigations and biomarkers in infective endocarditis (IE) yield non-specific results; markers such as C-reactive protein and procalcitonin can assess sepsis severity but lack sufficient accuracy or specificity for IE diagnosis. Microbiological diagnosis of IE relies on blood cultures: at least three sets should be obtained before antibiotics, with cultures incubated in aerobic and anaerobic conditions and organisms identified rapidly (e.g., Gram staining, MALDI-TOF MS) to guide antibiotic therapy. content.narrative_summary: Continued discussion of antimicrobial therapy for infective endocarditis. The POET trial supports a two-phase approach: an early critical phase of up to 2 weeks of inpatient intravenous bactericidal therapy with possible cardiac surgery, device removal, and abscess drainage, followed by a continuation phase of outpatient IV or oral antibiotic treatment (OPAT) for up to 6 weeks to eradicate resting bacteria. content.title: 7.8. Enterococcus spp.
content.narrative_summary: Enterococcal infective endocarditis is most often caused by E. faecalis (∼90%) and less commonly by E. faecium or other species. Eradication requires prolonged (up to 6 weeks) synergistic bactericidal combinations: two cell-wall inhibitors (ampicillin plus ceftriaxone) or one cell-wall inhibitor with an aminoglycoside. Penicillin-susceptible strains are treated with penicillin G or ampicillin (or amoxicillin) plus gentamicin, but high-level aminoglycoside resistance (HLAR; MIC >128 mg/L) negates synergism and precludes aminoglycoside use. Recent cohort studies in non-HLAR E. faecalis support ampicillin plus ceftriaxone as equally effective to ampicillin plus gentamicin, with a better safety profile and allowance for shorter gentamicin duration (2 weeks) and single daily dosing. In clinically stable patients, OPAT or outpatient oral therapy may be considered after 10–14 days. Beta-lactam or vancomycin resistance is mainly observed in E. faecium; daptomycin (10–12 mg/kg/24 h) combined with beta-lactams or fosfomycin is recommended for multidrug- and vancomycin-resistant strains.

content.narrative_summary: The page discusses surgical management of infective endocarditis (IE), including indications for urgent, emergency, and non-urgent surgery as defined by the Task Force. Pre-operative risk assessment is influenced by co-morbidities and organ function, with decisions made by an Endocarditis Team. Various scoring systems (AEPEI, STS, PALSUSE, EuroSCORE, Feo score, ANCLA) predict post-surgical mortality but require further clinical validation. Heart failure is noted as the most frequent IE complication and a primary indication for urgent surgery, with variable prevalence in left-sided IE.

content.title: Recommendation Table 12 — Recommendations for the main indications of surgery in infective endocarditis (native valve endocarditis and prosthetic valve endocarditis)
content.narrative_summary: Neurological manifestations may occur before or after IE diagnosis, with symptomatic cerebrovascular events in up to 35% of patients and silent ischaemic or microhaemorrhages in up to 80%. Presentations range from ischaemic stroke and transient ischaemic attack to intracerebral haemorrhage, meningitis, brain abscess, and encephalopathy. Staphylococcus aureus IE more frequently leads to neurological complications; larger and more mobile vegetations increase embolic risk. Early diagnosis, prompt antibiotic therapy, and timely cardiac surgery in high-risk patients help prevent embolization, while mechanical thrombectomy and anticoagulation are considered individually. Recommendations for neurological complications management are summarized in the following Table 13.

It defines cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) infections as superficial pocket or hardware infections and systemic infections, describes local seeding and bacteraemia mechanisms, and lists common organisms including CoNS, S. aureus, streptococci, Enterococcus spp., and rare fungal or polymicrobial agents. Prophylaxis recommendations cover pre-operative antibiotics (e.g., flucloxacillin, cefazolin; vancomycin if allergic), attention to modifiable risks, and use of antibiotic envelopes. Diagnosis of CIED-associated IE parallels valvular IE, with pocket signs and culture positivity influenced by organism type.

section_headings: 12.5. Infective endocarditis in patients admitted to intensive care units
content.narrative_summary: Infective endocarditis requiring ICU admission is associated with high mortality (in-hospital rates of ~32–42%), driven by factors including advanced age, high severity scores (SAPS II >35, SOFA >8), organ failure, stroke, MRSA infection, and native valve involvement. Staphylococcus spp., particularly S. aureus, are the predominant pathogens, with Streptococcus, Enterococcus, Gram-negative bacilli, and Candida also implicated. Diagnosis may be delayed in ICU patients due to atypical presentations and requires echocardiography (including TOE) and molecular methods when blood cultures are negative. Management involves antimicrobial therapy and, in about half of ICU patients, surgical intervention—though surgery carries increased peri-operative risk requiring close circulatory support and goal-directed therapy. Right-sided IE accounts for 5–10% of cases, with rising incidence among patients with CHD, indwelling catheters, CIEDs, immunocompromise, and PWID.

rows.recommendation: Complete CIED extraction should be considered in case of valvular IE, even without definite lead involvement, taking into account the identified pathogen and requirement for valve surgery.

In cases of possible CIED-related IE with occult Gram-positive bacteremia or fungemia, complete system removal should be considered in case bacteraemia/fungaemia persists after a course of antimicrobial therapy.
Extension of antibiotic treatment of CIED-related endocarditis to (4–6) weeks following device extraction should be considered in the presence of septic emboli or prosthetic valves.
Use of an antibiotic envelope may be considered in select high-risk patients undergoing CIED reimplantation to reduce risk of infection.

In cases of possible CIED-related IE with occult Gram-negative bacteraemia, complete system removal may be considered in case of persistent/relapsing bacteremia after a course of antimicrobial therapy.

In non-S. aureus CIED-related endocarditis without valve involvement or lead vegetations, and if follow-up blood cultures are negative without septic emboli, 2 weeks of antibiotic treatment may be considered following device extraction.
Removal of CIED after a single positive blood culture, with no other clinical evidence of infection, is not recommended.

section_headings: 12.6.2. Endocarditis in people who inject drugs
content.narrative_summary: This section discusses right-sided infective endocarditis (IE), most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus affecting the tricuspid valve. Diagnosis relies on echocardiography (TTE and TOE), supplemented by 18F-FDG-PET and CT when needed. In people who inject drugs (PWID), right-sided IE incidence is rising, often successfully treated medically despite high recurrence. Overall prognosis of right-sided IE is more benign than left-sided; CIED-related cases and immunocompromised patients have worse outcomes. Empirical antimicrobial therapy should cover S. aureus with penicillinase-resistant penicillins, vancomycin, or daptomycin, and consider anti-Pseudomonas or antifungals in PWID. Treatment duration varies with organism, vegetation size, clinical response, and presence of complications. Surgical indications include persistent bacteremia after ≥1 week of antibiotics, severe tricuspid regurgitation unresponsive to diuretics, respiratory insufficiency from recurrent pulmonary emboli, left-sided involvement, and large residual vegetations (>20 mm). Patients should be evaluated by the Endocarditis Team.

Section 14 highlights that female sex is less common in infective endocarditis (IE), representing about one-third of cases. The reasons for this sex discrepancy are unclear and may include underdiagnosis in women, referral bias, intrinsic protective mechanisms, and lower incidence of certain risk factors (e.g., bicuspid aortic valve disease, previous valve surgery). A nationwide Scottish study of 7,513 IE patients showed roughly equal male and female proportions over 25 years. Women with IE have higher prevalence of older age, mitral valve involvement, Staphylococcus aureus infection, neurological symptoms, and haemodialysis, while men have more prosthetic valve replacements, periannular complications, coronary artery disease, and cirrhosis. Studies differ on whether female sex is associated with higher mortality.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents multiple sections of Class of Recommendation (COR) and Level of Evidence (LOE) recommendations for the management of infective endocarditis. It covers outpatient antibiotic therapy, indications for surgery in native and prosthetic valve endocarditis (including specific sub‐indications: heart failure, uncontrolled infection, prevention of embolism), treatment of neurologic and musculoskeletal complications, pre-operative coronary anatomy assessment, timing of surgery after neurologic events, post-discharge follow-up, prosthetic valve endocarditis, and device-related infective endocarditis. The table continues on the next page.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for outpatient antibiotic treatment of infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: Outpatient parenteral antibiotic treatment is not recommended in patients with IE caused by highly difficult-to-treat microorganisms, liver cirrhosis (Child–Pugh B or C), severe cerebral nervous system emboli, untreated large extracardiac abscesses, heart valve complications, or other severe conditions requiring surgery, severe post-surgical complications, and PWID-related IE.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the main indications of surgery in infective endocarditis (native valve endocarditis and prosthetic valve endocarditis)

rows.recommendation: Emergency surgery is recommended in aortic or mitral NVE or PVE with severe acute regurgitation, obstruction, or fistula causing refractory pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock.
Urgent surgery is recommended in aortic or mitral NVE or PVE with severe acute regurgitation or obstruction causing symptoms of HF or echocardiographic signs of poor haemodynamic tolerance.
Urgent surgery is recommended in locally uncontrolled infection (abscess, false aneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation, prosthetic dehiscence, new AVB).
Urgent or non-urgent surgery is recommended in IE caused by fungi or multiresistant organisms according to the haemodynamic condition of the patient.
Urgent surgery is recommended in aortic or mitral NVE or PVE with persistent vegetations ≥10 mm after one or more embolic episodes despite appropriate antibiotic therapy.
Urgent surgery is recommended in IE with vegetation ≥10 mm and other indications for surgery.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the treatment of neurological complications of infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: Brain CT or MRA is recommended in patients with IE and suspected infective cerebral aneurysms.
Neurosurgery or endovascular therapy is recommended for large aneurysms, those with continuous growth despite optimal antibiotic therapy, and ruptured intracranial infective cerebral aneurysms.
Thrombolytic therapy is not recommended in embolic stroke due to IE.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for patients with musculoskeletal manifestations of infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: MRI or PET/CT is recommended in patients with suspected spondylodiscitis and vertebral osteomyelitis complicating IE.
TTE/TOE is recommended to rule out IE in patients with spondylodiscitis and/or septic arthritis with positive blood cultures for typical IE microorganisms.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for pre-operative coronary anatomy assessment in patients requiring surgery for infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: In haemodynamically stable patients with aortic valve vegetations who require cardiac surgery and are high risk of CAD, a high-resolution multislice coronary CTA is recommended.
Invasive coronary angiography is recommended in patients requiring heart surgery who are high risk of CAD, in the absence of aortic valve vegetations.

recommendation_tables.title: Indications and timing of cardiac surgery after neurological complications in active infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: After a transient ischaemic attack, cardiac surgery, if indicated, is recommended without delay.

After a stroke, surgery is recommended without any delay in the presence of HF, uncontrolled infection, abscess, or persistent high embolic risk, as long as coma is absent and the presence of cerebral haemorrhage has been excluded by cranial CT or MRI.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for post-discharge follow-up

rows.recommendation: Patient education on the risk of recurrence and preventive measures, with emphasis on dental health, and based on the individual risk profile is recommended during follow-up.
Addiction treatment for patients following PWID-related IE is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for prosthetic valve endocarditis

rows.recommendation: Surgery is recommended for early PVE (within 6 months of valve surgery) with new valve replacement and complete debridement.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for cardiovascular implanted electronic device-related infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: Antibiotic prophylaxis covering S. aureus is recommended for CIED implantation.
TTE and TOE are both recommended in cases of suspected CIED-related IE to identify vegetations.
Complete system extraction without delay is recommended in patients with definite CIED-related IE under initial empirical antibiotic therapy.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents three recommendation tables: management of cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) infection, surgical treatment of right-sided infective endocarditis, and use of antithrombotic therapy in infective endocarditis. An abbreviation legend follows. Sections 18–20 provide information on supplementary data availability, data availability statement, and author affiliations.

rows.recommendation: Obtaining at least three sets of blood cultures is recommended before prompt initiation of empirical antibiotic therapy for CIED infection, covering methicillin-resistant staphylococci and Gram-negative bacteria.

If CIED reimplantation is indicated after extraction for CIED-related IE, it is recommended to be performed at a site distant from the previous generator, as late as possible, once signs and symptoms of infection have abated, and until blood cultures are negative for at least 72 h in the absence of vegetations, and negative for at least 2 weeks if vegetations were visualized.
Removal of CIED after a single positive blood culture, with no other clinical evidence of infection, is not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the surgical treatment of right-sided infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: Right ventricular dysfunction secondary to acute severe tricuspid regurgitation non-responsive to diuretics.
Persistent vegetation with respiratory insufficiency requiring ventilatory support after recurrent pulmonary emboli.
Large residual tricuspid vegetations (>20 mm) after recurrent septic pulmonary emboli.
Patients with simultaneous involvement of left-heart structures.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the use of antithrombotic therapy in infective endocarditis

rows.recommendation: Interruption of antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy is recommended in the presence of major bleeding (including intracranial haemorrhage).
Thrombolytic therapy is not recommended in patients with IE.
